translations.text: By Saint Basil, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
Praise of the Forty Martyrs. At the commemoration of the martyrs, how can those who love the martyrs ever have enough?
For honoring good fellow servants is also a demonstration of love for the common Master.
It is clear that those who praise brave men in comparable circumstances
will not fail to imitate them. Therefore sincerely call blessed the one who has suffered martyrdom, so that you may be a martyr by your own choice,
and emerge without persecution, without fire, without being flayed, deemed worthy of those same sufferings.
But our task is to marvel not at one martyr, nor at two,
nor at ten. The number of the blessed is forty men, who have, as though they were one, a single soul
in separate bodies, but share one spirit and unity of faith.
They also displayed the same endurance in the face of cruelties and the same steadfastness in defense of the truth.
All were alike, equal to one another, equal in their resolve and in their suffering.
Therefore they were also deemed worthy of an equally honored crown of glory. What speech, then, could adequately praise them?
Not even forty tongues would suffice to sing of such great virtue in these men.
Even if there were only one to admire, he would be enough to surpass our powers, let alone so great a multitude. [?]
[?], an invincible army, likewise undefeated in battle.
Let us then bring them into our midst through remembrance, and prepare a common benefit
from them for those present, first displaying to everyone,
as in a picture, the courage of these men and their prowess in battle.
For writers and painters often make depictions, the former embellishing with words,
and the latter drawing on panels; both have spurred many to courage.
For what speech makes known through narration and hearing, books also show silently through representation.
Likewise, let us recall the virtue of these men to those present,
so that, placing their deeds before our eyes, we may be moved to imitate these supremely brave men
and draw closer to them through imitation. For the praise of martyrs is the encouragement of those gathered
toward virtue. For speeches about the saints do not seek to be governed by the rules of praise.
For those who offer praise draw the beginnings of their praises from the things of this world.
But for those to whom the world has been crucified, how can anything in it add to their glory?
For the saints did not all have the same homeland: one came from one
land, another from another. So what shall we now call them: people without a city, or citizens of the whole world?
For just as, when people gather to make an offering, what each person brings becomes common to all who have brought offerings,
so also with these blessed men: each one's homeland belongs to them all.
And they all belong everywhere, granting one another a homeland. Or rather, why do we seek a city among those that stand
on the earth, leaving aside their present city, which is spiritual?
The martyrs' city is the city of God, whose architect and builder is God:
the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free, the mother of Paul and those like him. As for human birth,
one comes from one place, another from another; but their spiritual birth is one and the same for all. For they have God as their common Father,
and they are all brothers, not born of one father and one mother, but through spiritual adoption,
having joined themselves together in a union of love: a company made ready, a great addition to those who have glorified the Lord from ages past.
They were not gathered one by one, but departed all at once. How did their departure take place?
These men, in bodily stature, youthful vigor, and strength, were, among all their peers,
superior; they were all enrolled in the army. And because of their skill in warfare
and their courage of soul, they received great honors from the emperor,
being renowned among all for their virtue. But when it had already been proclaimed—
when that godless and impious proclamation had already been issued,
forbidding them to name Christ, on pain of suffering, every kind of torture was threatened,
and great, beastlike fury arose among the unrighteous against the faithful.
Plots and evil plans were woven against them, and various kinds of torture were devised.
And those being tortured did not weaken. Fire was ready, the sword sharpened, the cross set up,
the abyss, the wheel, clubs. And some fled, while others obeyed.
Some wavered; others were frightened by the mere threat of trial; still others, coming close to the horrors, gave way.
Others, however, entered the contest, but could not endure the suffering to the end.
They renounced their faith in the midst of suffering, like those struggling in the open sea,
and lost the cargo of endurance they possessed. Then these invincible
and valiant soldiers of Christ stepped forward while the governor was displaying the emperor’s decrees
and demanding obedience from everyone. With an unrestrained voice, boldly and courageously,
not at all frightened by the threats, they stepped into the midst and declared themselves Christians.
O blessed tongues, all those that uttered that holy cry!
The air received it and was sanctified, and the angels heard it and clapped their hands.
The devil and his demons were wounded, and the Lord wrote their names in heaven.
Each of them, then, stepped into the midst and said, “I am a Christian.”
Just as those entering battle all announce their names
and step onto the battlefield, so these men, too, cast aside the names given to them
at birth, and each named himself after the Savior of all.
They all did this, joining themselves together one after another, so that they all had one name.
For they were no longer called by this or that name, but were all called Christians.
But what did that ruler do then? For he was cruel and divided: at one moment he soothed them with flattery,
and at another he sought to turn them aside with threats. First, then, he enticed them with flattery,
trying to weaken their steadfastness in the good faith. “Do not throw away your youth,” he said, “nor be willing to exchange for an untimely
death this sweet life. It is not fitting for those accustomed to victory in battle
to die a criminal’s death.” Besides this, he also promised gifts.
And furthermore, “[?] you will receive honors from the emperor and high offices.” And with countless schemes
he flattered them. But when they did not weaken under this temptation, he turned to another kind of scheme.
He assailed them with wounds, deaths, and immeasurable tortures. Such were the words he spoke.
But what were the martyrs’ words? “Why,” they said, “do you entice us, you enemy of God, to abandon the living God
and serve destructive demons, setting your good things before us? What can you give that is so great?
Whatever you strive to take away. I hate such a gift, which brings loss. I do not accept honor that is the mother of dishonor.
Do you give gifts that pass away, or glory that passes away? Do you make me known to the emperor?
But you lead me away from the true King. Why do you speak of little things and give little things from this world?
We care nothing for the whole world. Visible things are not equal to the hope we long for.
Do you see this heaven, how beautiful it is to behold and how vast, and the earth, how great it is,
and all the wonderful things upon it? None of all these things is equal to the blessedness
of the righteous. For these things pass away, but ours endure. I long for one gift: the crown of righteousness.
I wish to see one glory, and the kingdom of heaven. I dearly love the honor from above.
I fear the torment of hell. I tremble at that fire.
But I do not fear what you threaten us with, for it is my fellow servant and knows how to respect
those who disregard idols. I regard your blows as children's arrows, for you strike the body.
If it endures courageously, it receives a more glorious crown. But if it dies suddenly,
it will depart, freed from oppressive judges. Who are you who, entrusted with service over the body,
attempt to rule over souls as well? Who are you to set yourselves above our God?
And when you receive even the slightest affront from us, you become indignant and threaten us with these terrible torments,
bringing our devotion to God against us as a sin. But those you threaten are not timid, frightened, or easily terrified.
For the love of God we are ready to be bound to the wheel, to be bound and burned,
and to undergo every kind of torture. When that arrogant and savage man heard these things,
unable to endure the men's boldness, he became still more savage with rage
and considered what device he could invent to make their
death prolonged. He devised a plan. See how cruel it was.
For he had observed the nature of that land, that the cold there was severe, and that the season was winter.
Having chosen a night when the cold was especially harsh, with a north wind also blowing that night,
he ordered them all to be stripped naked and to freeze to death in the open in the middle of the city.
But all of you who have experienced winter know how severe this kind of torture is.
For it cannot be explained to anyone but those who have experienced it. For when the body falls into the cold,
at first it turns entirely blue, as the blood congeals.
Then it becomes agitated and seethes, the teeth chattering and the sinews contracting,
and the whole body convulsing involuntarily. Sudden, fierce, indescribable pain,
reaching the very limbs, makes sensation painful for those exposed to the frost. Then the extremities fall off
the body, as though burned by fire. For the heat, driven away from the body's extremities
and fleeing into its depths, leaves dead the parts from which it has withdrawn,
and brings pain into those it enters, as death gradually comes through the frost. Then they were sentenced
to stand in the open all night, while a fierce north wind blew without ceasing.
There was a lake beside which the city had been built, where these saints suffered.
It had become like a plain for horses to run on, the frost having transformed it and frozen it solid.
People on foot and on horseback traveled over it. The ever-flowing rivers froze and stood still, and the soft substance of water
was transformed into something resembling stone. The fierce north wind blew, driving everything that had breath toward death.
Then, when they heard the command—consider here, I ask you, how unconquerable the men were—with joy,
each throwing off even his last tunic, they went toward death by freezing as though going to seize riches,
encouraging one another and saying: “Are we merely stripping off clothes? No, we are putting off the old man,
corrupted by deceitful desires. We praise you, Lord, stripping sin from ourselves along with this garment.
Since we clothed ourselves because of the serpent, let us strip ourselves for Christ's sake. Let us not spare our clothes for the sake of the paradise we lost.
What shall I give back to the Lord? Our Lord too was stripped. What great thing is it for a servant to undergo the same thing as his Lord?
Indeed, we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord. For [?] dared to do it.
They stripped him and divided his clothes. Let us, then, put away through ourselves the great reproach recorded against us.
The winter is fierce, but paradise is sweet. Freezing is painful, but rest is pleasant. Let us wait a little,
and the bosom of the patriarch Abraham will shelter us. Let us exchange one night for all eternity.
Let the foot be burned, so that it may dance forever with the angels. Let the hand be cut off,
so that it may have the confidence to be raised to the Master. How many of our [?] have fallen in battle!
keeping faith with a mortal king. But we, for the sake of friendship with the true King—
will I not give up this life? How many have suffered a criminal’s death after being arrested for wrongdoing!
But will we not endure for righteousness? Let us not shrink from death, which is common to us all.
Let us not give the devil [?]. Let us not spare our flesh [?]. For since we must all die,
let us die so that we may live. Let our bodies be a sacrifice before you, Lord, and let us be accepted
as a living sacrifice pleasing to you, consumed by this cold: a good offering, a new burnt offering,
sacrificed neither by fire nor by cold. Offering these comforting words to one another
and encouraging one another, acting as though they were keeping watch in battle, they passed the night,
enduring their suffering, rejoicing courageously in what they hoped for, and mocking the adversary.
They all had one prayer: “Forty of us entered this struggle; let forty of us be crowned, Master.
Let not even one be missing from our number. Honored is the number that you have honored
with forty days of fasting, through which the Law came into the world. Through forty days of fasting,
Elijah sought the Lord and saw the Lord.” Such was their prayer. But one of their number grew weak
in the face of the harsh suffering and fled, leaving immeasurable sorrow to the saints. The Lord allowed their prayers to remain unfulfilled.
For the man appointed to guard the martyrs was warming himself nearby in a bathhouse, watching what would happen,
ready to receive any of them [?] who fled to him. For this too had been devised:
a bathhouse nearby, offering swift help to those who fled there. This too had been
cunningly devised by the evildoers: to find such a place, where readily available relief would weaken
the endurance of those engaged in the struggle. Yet this made all the more glorious
the endurance of the martyrs. For it is not the person who lacks necessities who is enduring,
but the one who has abundance and yet endures suffering. And so, while
they struggled and he kept watch, he saw a wondrous vision unfolding:
heavenly powers descending from heaven and distributing great gifts to them [?], as though from the King.
They gave gifts to everyone, leaving only one without honor,
saying that he was unworthy of heavenly honors—the one who immediately failed to endure the pain.
He fled to the enemy. A dreadful sight for the righteous: a brave soldier who deserted,
a captive, a sheep of Christ, prey for wild beasts. And what is more wretched,
he missed out on heavenly life and did not enjoy this life either. At once, at the touch of warmth,
his flesh melted away. The man who loved life collapsed, having broken the law in vain.
But when the guard saw that he had turned aside and run into the bathhouse,
he placed himself in the deserter’s place. Throwing off his clothes, he joined the naked men,
crying out the same declaration as the saints: “I am a Christian!” And by the suddenness of his change,
he became a wonder to those watching. He filled up their number, and the sorrow that had arisen
over the man who had fled he relieved by adding himself, imitating the fighters in the front ranks,
who immediately fill the [?] left by a man who has fallen in the foremost line of shields, so that their front is not thrown into confusion by the fallen man. The same thing
he too did. He saw heavenly wonders, recognized the truth, ran to the Lord, and was numbered among the martyrs.
He renewed what had happened among the disciples: Judas departed, and Matthias entered in his place. He became an imitator of Paul:
yesterday a persecutor, today a preacher of the gospel. He too received his calling from above,
not from men or through a man. He believed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and was baptized into him,
not by Paul, but by his own faith; not in water, but in his own blood. And so, as day began,
they were all handed over to the fire while still breathing, and the remains left by the fire were poured into the river,
so that the suffering of the blessed might pass through all creation. They struggled on earth; they endured the cold;
they were handed over to fire; water received them. Theirs is the voice that says, “We passed through fire and water,
and you brought us out to a place of refreshment.” These are the men who have embraced our land, like sons of an allotted inheritance,
holding back invasions by enemies. They have not confined themselves to one place,
but are present in many places and have adorned many homelands. And this is glorious:
they have not been divided up one by one among those who receive them, but, mingled together, they rejoice as one.
What a wonder! They are neither fewer in number nor do they become more numerous. Even if you divide them into a hundred portions, their own
number does not change. If you gather them into one place, they remain forty even so, in keeping with the nature of fire.
For fire passes to what is being kindled, yet remains whole with the one who has it.
and forty. And all are together, and all are with each person: an ungrudging gift.
Inexhaustible grace, ready help for Christians, an assembly of martyrs, victorious warriors,
a company of those who sing praise. How hard you would work to find somehow even one person praying to the Lord for you!
There are forty sending up prayer with one accord. Where two or three are gathered
in the Lord’s name, there he is among them. But where there are forty, who would now argue
that God is not present there? Let anyone who grieves take refuge with the forty.
Anyone who rejoices runs to them: the one to escape sorrow,
and the other so that his joy may be preserved. Here a faithful woman comes, praying for her children; when her husband is going away,
she prays for his return, and for recovery for someone who is sick. Let your petitions be with the martyrs.
Let young people imitate those of their own age, and let fathers pray to be fathers of such children.
And let mothers learn the story of the good mother. The mother of one of those blessed men, seeing
the others already dead from the cold, but her own son still breathing,
because of his strength and endurance of the harsh suffering, while the rulers were leaving him behind,
as though he might somehow change his mind, herself lifted him onto her shoulder with her own hands and placed him on the cart
on which the others lay as they were being taken to the fire. Truly a martyr’s mother!
For she shed no tear of weakness, nor did she say anything abject or unworthy of the occasion.
Instead she said, “Go, my son, on your good journey, with those of your own age and with your companions.
Do not separate yourself from the company. Do not appear before the Master after the others.” Truly, from a good root came a good shoot.
The brave mother showed that she had nourished him with the teachings of the true faith even more than with milk.
Having been brought up in this way, he was sent on his way like this by his faithful mother. And the devil went away in shame.
For although he had stirred up all creation against them, he found it all overcome by the virtue of these men:
the fiercely windy night, the frozen ground, the season, the nakedness of their bodies.
O holy company! O sacred assembly! O invincible [?]!
O guardians of the whole human race, good companions in sorrow, helpers in
prayer, stars of the world, flowers of the Church! The earth has not covered you, nor has heaven received you.
The gates of paradise opened—a sight worthy of the angelic hosts,
worthy of the patriarchs, prophets, and righteous men. Men in the very flower of youth,
disregarding their lives, loving the Lord more than their parents, more than their children, bearing the [?] of life itself,
they despised this temporary life so that they might glorify God in their bodies.
Having become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings, they raised up those who had fallen.
They strengthened those who doubted and doubled the longing of the faithful.
They all held up a single victory—the good faith—and with one and the same crown
of righteousness they adorned themselves in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
